title: Spreadsheet With Live Sum Formulas
statement:
Build a tiny spreadsheet. Rows are numbered from 1 to height, columns are letters from 'A' to width. Every cell starts at 0.

  • Excel(height, width) creates the sheet.
  • set(row, column, val) puts the plain number val in the cell. If the cell held a formula, the formula is removed.
  • get(row, column) returns the cell's current value.
  • sum(row, column, numbers) turns the cell into a formula and returns its value. Each entry of numbers is a single cell like "B3" or a rectangle like "A1:C2" (top-left to bottom-right). The cell's value is the sum of all referenced cells; a cell that is referenced twice is counted twice.

A formula is live: when any cell it depends on changes, directly or through other formulas, its value changes too. Formulas never form a cycle.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the sheet. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for Excel and set).

examples.why: B2 sums A1 and B1. Setting B1 to 3 later changes B2 from 5 to 8 without another call to sum.
A2 counts A1 twice. Then set replaces A2's formula with a plain 10, so later changes to A1 reach A3 only directly: 4 + 10.

constraints: width is a letter from 'A' to 'Z'
Formulas never form a cycle, and every value fits in a 32-bit signed integer
hints: A formula cell must change when something it depends on changes. Either recompute it when it is read, or push changes forward when they happen. Which is simpler?
Store each formula as a map from referenced cell to how many times it is referenced (ranges expanded). A plain cell is just a number.

Pull model: get evaluates recursively, summing count × value of each reference, with a memo per call. Push model: keep reverse edges (who depends on me); after a change, recompute the affected formulas in topological order.

explain.intuition:
The cells and formulas form a dependency graph with no cycles, the same structure as a reactive UI framework's computed values or a build tool's file graph. A formula cell is a node whose value is Σ count × value over the cells it references, where count is how many times a reference appears after expanding ranges.

There are two classic strategies. Pull: store only the formulas and compute a cell's value when it is read, recursing into referenced formulas; a memo for the duration of one read makes shared dependencies cheap. Push: store every value, keep reverse edges from each cell to the formulas that use it, and after a set or sum recompute every affected formula in topological order, so each one sees already-updated inputs. Pull makes writes cheap; push makes reads cheap. Both are correct because the graph has no cycles.
steps: Index cells as (row − 1) × 26 + column. Keep value[cell] and formula[cell] (a map of referenced cell → count, or nothing).
sum: expand each entry of numbers into cells and count them. Store this as the cell's formula, then return its value.
set: drop the cell's formula and store the plain number.
get (pull version): if the cell has a formula, return Σ count × get(ref) using a memo shared within this call; otherwise return the stored number.
pitfalls: Computing a formula once and storing the number. Formulas are live and must follow later changes, as in the first example.
Collapsing duplicate references into a set. ["A1", "A1"] counts A1 twice.
Forgetting that set on a formula cell removes its formula, so it stops reacting to its old inputs.
Pushing a delta along every path without ordering. With shared dependencies (a diamond) the work can explode; recompute in topological order instead.

complexity.time: Pull: O(1) set, sum O(cells referenced), get O(formulas and references reachable). Push: get O(1), set and sum O(affected formulas and their references)

solutions.title: Pull: evaluate formulas on read
solutions.idea: Keep plain values and formulas. get walks the formula graph recursively, with a memo for the current call so shared inputs are computed once.
solutions.time: get O(reachable references), set and sum as cheap as parsing

solutions.title: Push: propagate changes in topological order
solutions.idea: Store every cell's current value and reverse edges to the formulas that use it. After a change, collect the affected formulas with a DFS, then recompute them in topological order.
solutions.time: get O(1), set and sum O(affected formulas and their references)

followups: A new formula may create a cycle. How do you detect it before accepting the formula?
Reads are rare and writes are very frequent. Which of the two designs would you pick, and how would you add caching to the other?
